cards.front: Recall a key point about International Trade
cards.back: Countries trade because of comparative advantage: each country specialises in goods where it has the lowest opportunity cost, then trades for other goods.

cards.front: Recall a key point about International Trade
cards.back: Benefits of trade: access to wider range of goods, lower prices through competition, larger markets for producers, spread of technology, and consumer choice.

cards.front: Recall a key point about International Trade
cards.back: The UK's main exports: financial services, pharmaceuticals, cars. Main imports: manufactured goods, food, fuel. Trade deficit in goods but surplus in services.

cards.front: Recall a key point about International Trade
cards.back: Free-trade agreements (like the EU) remove tariffs and quotas between members, increasing trade and competition. The EU was the UK's largest trading partner.

cards.front: Recall a key point about International Trade
cards.back: Arguments against free trade: domestic industries may be undercut (job losses), dependency on foreign suppliers, loss of economic sovereignty, and trade deficits.

cards.front: What should you know about economics exam tips?
cards.back: When evaluating international trade, use the CAB framework: Comparative advantage, Adjustment costs (who loses, and can they transition?), Benefits (lower prices, more choice, export markets).
Lower (competition from imports) (e.g. Higher (tariffs and restricted supply))
Greater access to global products (e.g. Limited to domestic production)
Jobs lost in uncompetitive sectors (e.g. Jobs protected in sheltered sectors)
Resources allocated by comparative advantage (e.g. Resources may be misallocated to protected sectors)
EU single market membership (pre-Brexit) (e.g. Post-Brexit customs barriers and checks)
None (mutual benefit) (e.g. Trade wars (e.g. US-China tariff escalations))

Students often make mistakes here. Wrong: Free trade always benefits every person in a country because prices fall. Correct: While free trade lowers average prices, it creates winners (consumers, exporters) and losers (workers in import-competing industries who may lose jobs).
